paper.title: Undeclared Danish Labor: Using the labor input method with linked individual-level tax data to estimate undeclared work in Denmark
paper.journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (journal p. 723, PDF p. 16): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' Declaration of Competing Interest: …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish Labor Force Survey (LFS; in Danish AKU), part of the EU LFS, administered by Statistics Denmark
registers.role: treatment / outcome / sample frame - actual hours worked in the reference week, agreed (contracted) hours, reasons for working more or fewer hours, overtime remuneration, form of employment, industry sector, secondary occupation, lunchbreak, and (in one round a year) a direct undeclared-work question
variables_mentioned: actual hours worked in the reference week
reason for working more or fewer hours
hours of overtime and how remunerated
form of employment (wage earner / self-employed / assisting spouse / contributing family worker)
whether a lunchbreak is included in contracted hours
direct question on undeclared work in the previous twelve months

registers.name_in_paper: eIncome (in Danish: eIndkomst) administrative tax data, reported to the tax administration by Danish businesses and delivered to Statistics Denmark
registers.role: treatment / outcome - administrative hours and salary reported monthly by employers; the benchmark against which the survey hours are differenced
variables_mentioned: imputation flag set by Statistics Denmark

registers.name_in_paper: tax returns of the self-employed (added anonymously to the dataset by Statistics Denmark)
registers.role: treatment - annual income used to impute administrative hours for the two thirds of non-wage earners without eIncome data
variables_mentioned: other income such as stocks and fringe benefits

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark National Accounts (statbank.dk/nabp19 gross value added; statbank.dk/nabb19 hours worked)
registers.role: controls / valuation - gross value added per full-time employee by industry sector used to value the undeclared hours (Table A4), and GDP for Table 9

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark internal imputation documentation 'Use Case 13: imputer løntimer (IML)' (Statistics Denmark, 2008)
registers.role: linkage / method - the twelve-level hot-decking and cold-decking imputation scheme reused by the paper

registers.name_in_paper: Danish Ministry of Taxation, 'Skattetrykket i Danmark' (2018)
registers.role: controls - average Danish tax rate used in the tax-gap calculation (49.80% in 2014, 47.40% in 2015)

linkages: Statistics Denmark combined the Danish Labor Force Survey with official eIncome tax data on hours worked reported by Danish businesses, and with income data from tax returns, at the individual level; the linked data was made anonymous and accessed via Statistics Denmark's remote server
Because the data are anonymous, unlike Paulus (2015) there is no selection bias from respondents choosing to have their survey data combined with tax data
Survey hours are matched to administrative hours per quarter: eIncome hours are summed to the quarter and the survey reference-week hours are multiplied by 13

Main and secondary occupations are matched separately; the administrative job with the highest number of hours per quarter is deemed the main occupation, and all secondary-occupation administrative hours are summed

sample.universe: Employed persons aged 15-74 resident in Denmark, drawn into the Danish Labor Force Survey four times a year in 2014 and 2015
sample.unit_of_observation: person-quarter (LFS respondent in a given survey quarter), aggregated to person-year for the annual estimates
selection_rules: Only people in the survey who are employed are included, defined as persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour
Statistics Denmark recommended using data for 2014 and 2015 because of changes to the LFS methodology in 2016
Cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (less than 1% of the employed population in the survey) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data
Assisting spouses (0.1%) and contributing family workers (0.2%) are grouped with the self-employed (9%) as non-wage earners

People who worked 0 actual LFS hours because they were on leave for the full reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation; only their secondary-occupation discrepancy is considered
Self-employed persons with no administrative hours and a negative income on their tax return (5% of non-wage earners) are assumed not to have worked undeclared
The method does not cover undocumented workers, cross-border workers living abroad, or undeclared work by people outside formal employment
sample.n_observations: approximately 14,000 employed Danish persons per quarter over eight quarters; the panel structure means the quarters are not independent (e.g. 6007 employed persons take part in both 2015.1 and 2015.2)
sample.n_individuals: approximately 60,000 unique employed persons: 54,000 wage earners and 6000 non-wage earners

construction_notes: Undeclared hours = corrected actual LFS hours (reference week x 13) minus corrected eIncome administrative hours for the quarter, computed separately for main and secondary occupation and combined under a four-case rule set (appendix, 'Methodology - calculating a discrepancy')

A person is recorded as not having worked undeclared if actual hours are 0; or actual hours in the main occupation are exactly 37 a week with no secondary-occupation hours; or actual hours are fewer than administrative hours +2; or a reason is stated for working more hours in the main occupation with no or fewer secondary-occupation hours; or the respondent was absent in the reference week with no secondary-occupation hours; or the respondent works in the public sector in main and secondary occupation; or the person is self-employed with no administrative hours and a negative tax-return income

Missing eIncome hours for wage earners (2.4%) are hot-decked on gender, scope of work, age group, workplace position, public/private sector, business sector and business size, following Statistics Denmark's own eIncome imputation; imputation groups require at least 50 people and are built from pooled 2014-2015 LFS data with one data point per person

Missing administrative hours for non-wage earners (60%) are calculated as Salaried hours = (salary / average hourly wage for group) * (calendar days in month / job length per month in calendar days), with 365 days substituted because tax returns are annual, the group defined by age and gender only, and group means taken from the 44% of non-wage earners who meet the imputation-group criteria; other income (stocks, fringe benefits) is removed to isolate a salary income

The most detailed imputation level attainable in the linked data is level 3 (gender, scope of work, age group, workplace position, public/private sector and two-digit business sector), reached for 68% of the employed population; level 4 for a further 9%; no imputation is done above level 9
Workplace position was reconstructed from ISCO codes as 1 = management, 2 = apprentices (under 21, in paid labor, not managers, in elementary occupations or armed forces), 3 = other employees

Legitimate overtime hours (the hours respondents allocate to a named form of overtime remuneration) are deducted from the survey hours before the discrepancy is calculated; 7-8% of the employed population worked overtime and the hours of the 2% who give no reason are left in
Hours of the self-employed are reduced by 9.8%, matching the negative adjustment Denmark makes in the National Accounts (OECD, 2018:42)

Extreme survey hours (above Statistics Denmark's 15 hours per day / 320 hours per month rule, about 75-80 hours a week) are replaced with imputed hours; the LFS imputation group is those working fewer than 60 hours per week (99% of wage earners, 92% of the self-employed)

Measurement error in the administrative hours is corrected by deducting, from each person's eIncome hours, the mean group difference between contracted LFS hours and eIncome hours measured among public-sector workers (level 8 groups for 88% of them)

Value added: estimated undeclared hours are valued with Statistics Denmark's gross value added per full-time employee by industry sector (Table A4); 'L. Real estate activities' and 'S. Other service activities' are each combined from two Statistics Denmark categories; the same value added per hour is applied to wage earners and non-wage earners; hours are allocated to the industry of the main occupation

Tax gap = gross value added x approximately one third (31% of purchasers say the work would have been done legitimately, Hvidtfeldt et al. 2010:237-239) x the average Danish tax rate (49.80% in 2014, 47.40% in 2015)
Results based on fewer than 20 respondents are suppressed (marked * in the tables) following Statistics Denmark guidelines, but the suppressed sectors are included in the reported totals
Administrative hours in secondary occupations are not corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method

All estimates use Statistics Denmark's LFS weights, which scale the quarterly data up to the general population and correct for the under-representation of 18-29 year olds caused by the research opt-out (forskerbeskyttelse) available until 2015

claims.statement: The labor input method applied to individual-level LFS data linked to eIncome tax data estimates that 29% of employed persons in Denmark in 2014-2015 have undeclared hours.

treatment.label: application of the labor input method to individual-level LFS data linked to eIncome administrative tax data, with all four corrections applied

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: Undeclared hours are measured as the discrepancy between the respondent's corrected actual hours in the LFS reference week (multiplied by 13 to represent a quarter) and the corrected eIncome administrative hours for the same quarter, after correcting for (1) missing administrative data, (2) legitimate overtime, (3) extreme values and (4) errors in the administrative data, and after removing respondents absent for the whole reference week

timing.value: LFS reference week of each of the eight quarters of 2014-2015, compared with eIncome hours for the same quarter

outcome.label: percentage of workers with undeclared work

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: LFS-weighted share of workers for whom the labor input discrepancy calculation yields a positive number of undeclared hours, i.e. more corrected actual LFS hours than corrected eIncome administrative hours in the main and/or secondary occupation

timing.value: per calendar year, pooling the four quarters of the year

units.value: percent of employed persons

estimand.target_population: employed persons aged 15-74 in Denmark in 2014-2015

population.description: Employed persons aged 15-74 interviewed in the Danish Labor Force Survey in 2014 and 2015 (approximately 14,000 employed respondents per quarter; approximately 60,000 unique employed persons in total), linked at the individual level to Danish eIncome administrative tax data and, for non-wage earners, to tax returns
subgroups_defined: wage earners
non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers)
industry sector of main occupation (NACE letter groups)
calendar quarter
population.selection: LFS respondents who are employed (persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour); cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (<1% of the employed population) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data; respondents absent for the whole reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

identification.source_of_variation: none - the estimate is a discrepancy between two measurements of the same person's hours (the LFS actual-hours answer and the eIncome hours reported by the employer), not exogenous variation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents have no reason to conceal their undeclared working hours in a household / labor force survey, so the hours they report include all hours worked, undeclared hours included
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the survey must be run by an institution unassociated with the tax authority, and notes that Statistics Denmark administers the Danish LFS and is completely unassociated with the tax office; it also notes that interviewers persist when a respondent answers 0 hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The residual between survey hours and administrative hours is assumed to represent undeclared working hours

The estimate is conditioned on being employed and registered in the official Danish population registers; the method does not cover undeclared work by populations outside formal employment, including undocumented workers, nor cross-border workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper bounds the size of the excluded undocumented population (Larsen and Skaksen 2019 estimate around 18,000 persons in 2015 against an employed population of about 2.5 million) and removes the under-1% of respondents who live in Denmark but work abroad

implies_edges.from: employed and registered in the Danish population registers
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents with fewer actual survey hours than administrative hours are assumed not to have worked any undeclared hours
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes the method cannot detect undeclared work for this group and accepts the resulting underestimation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who state flexible / shifting working hours as the reason for additional hours are assumed to be working legitimately, so their additional hours are not counted as undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: Looking at the direct measure of undeclared work in the survey, this group of people are not more likely to have engaged in undeclared work

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who worked 0 actual LFS hours because they were on leave for the whole reference week are removed from the discrepancy calculation (only their secondary-occupation discrepancy is considered)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows in Table A3 that in 2015.3 there are more administrative hours than survey hours, and accepts that the estimate may be underestimated for this population

implies_edges.from: absence for the whole LFS reference week
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

key_assumptions.assumption: All respondents who specify a reason for their legitimate overtime are assumed not to be working undeclared; the hours of the remaining 2% are assumed to be undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: After the correction, 98% of those with overtime have the same number of hours in eIncome as their reported actual worked hours; the paper calls this a conservative estimate because it cannot assess whether the stated reasons are correct

key_assumptions.assumption: The gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome hours among public-sector workers does not capture undeclared work on the employer's side, so it can serve as a benchmark for measurement error in the administrative data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues there is no reason for public employers to underreport hours and salaries of wage earners to the tax authorities, and that it can be said with relative certainty that this discrepancy does not capture employer-side undeclared work

implies_edges.from: employer-side undeclared work
implies_edges.to: public-sector gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome administrative hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The imputed administrative hours recover the hours that would have been reported for wage earners with missing eIncome data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper uses Statistics Denmark's own imputation method (hot-decking on group characteristics for wage earners; a salary-based hours calculation from tax returns for non-wage earners) and reports the level of detail attained

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed respondents with no administrative hours and a negative income on their tax return (5% of non-wage earners) are assumed not to have worked undeclared
The hours of the self-employed are overestimated in the survey by 9.8%, the negative adjustment Denmark applies to the reported hours of the self-employed in the National Accounts
key_assumptions.supported_by: OECD (2018:42): Denmark is one of five OECD countries that make negative adjustments to the reported hours of the self-employed

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours
Extreme survey values: under 1% of the sample works 75 or more hours a week and respondents, especially the self-employed, tend to overestimate hours
Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered
For the 10% of the employed population with flexible working hours and more actual than contracted hours, official additional hours cannot be disentangled from undeclared hours
Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week
Industry coding of undeclared work rests on the respondent's own description of the workplace and on the main occupation

The paper prints no estimating equation for this quantity.

treatment.label: application of the labor input method to individual-level LFS data linked to eIncome administrative tax data, with all four corrections applied

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: Undeclared hours are measured as the discrepancy between the respondent's corrected actual hours in the LFS reference week (multiplied by 13 to represent a quarter) and the corrected eIncome administrative hours for the same quarter, after correcting for (1) missing administrative data, (2) legitimate overtime, (3) extreme values and (4) errors in the administrative data, and after removing respondents absent for the whole reference week

timing.value: LFS reference week of each of the eight quarters of 2014-2015, compared with eIncome hours for the same quarter

outcome.label: gross value added of the undeclared hours of wage earners, in million DKK at current prices

register_source.value: estimated undeclared hours (LFS linked to eIncome) valued with Statistics Denmark National Accounts: gross value added by sector (statbank.dk/nabp19) and total hours worked (statbank.dk/nabb19)

definition.value: The estimated undeclared hours of wage earners are multiplied by Statistics Denmark's National Accounts gross value added per full-time employee by industry sector (Table A4); the same value added per hour is applied to wage earners and non-wage earners

timing.value: per calendar year, current prices

units.value: million DKK, current prices

estimand.target_population: wage earners aged 15-74 in Denmark in 2015

population.description: Wage earners among the employed respondents of the Danish Labor Force Survey 2014-2015 (approximately 54,000 unique persons; 91% of the employed population), linked to eIncome administrative tax data
subgroups_defined: wage earners
non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers)
industry sector of main occupation (NACE letter groups)
calendar quarter
population.selection: LFS respondents who are employed (persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour); cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (<1% of the employed population) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data; respondents absent for the whole reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

identification.source_of_variation: none - the estimate is a discrepancy between two measurements of the same person's hours (the LFS actual-hours answer and the eIncome hours reported by the employer), not exogenous variation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents have no reason to conceal their undeclared working hours in a household / labor force survey, so the hours they report include all hours worked, undeclared hours included
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the survey must be run by an institution unassociated with the tax authority, and notes that Statistics Denmark administers the Danish LFS and is completely unassociated with the tax office; it also notes that interviewers persist when a respondent answers 0 hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The residual between survey hours and administrative hours is assumed to represent undeclared working hours

The estimate is conditioned on being employed and registered in the official Danish population registers; the method does not cover undeclared work by populations outside formal employment, including undocumented workers, nor cross-border workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper bounds the size of the excluded undocumented population (Larsen and Skaksen 2019 estimate around 18,000 persons in 2015 against an employed population of about 2.5 million) and removes the under-1% of respondents who live in Denmark but work abroad

implies_edges.from: employed and registered in the Danish population registers
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents with fewer actual survey hours than administrative hours are assumed not to have worked any undeclared hours
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes the method cannot detect undeclared work for this group and accepts the resulting underestimation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who state flexible / shifting working hours as the reason for additional hours are assumed to be working legitimately, so their additional hours are not counted as undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: Looking at the direct measure of undeclared work in the survey, this group of people are not more likely to have engaged in undeclared work

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who worked 0 actual LFS hours because they were on leave for the whole reference week are removed from the discrepancy calculation (only their secondary-occupation discrepancy is considered)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows in Table A3 that in 2015.3 there are more administrative hours than survey hours, and accepts that the estimate may be underestimated for this population

implies_edges.from: absence for the whole LFS reference week
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

key_assumptions.assumption: All respondents who specify a reason for their legitimate overtime are assumed not to be working undeclared; the hours of the remaining 2% are assumed to be undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: After the correction, 98% of those with overtime have the same number of hours in eIncome as their reported actual worked hours; the paper calls this a conservative estimate because it cannot assess whether the stated reasons are correct

key_assumptions.assumption: The gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome hours among public-sector workers does not capture undeclared work on the employer's side, so it can serve as a benchmark for measurement error in the administrative data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues there is no reason for public employers to underreport hours and salaries of wage earners to the tax authorities, and that it can be said with relative certainty that this discrepancy does not capture employer-side undeclared work

implies_edges.from: employer-side undeclared work
implies_edges.to: public-sector gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome administrative hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The imputed administrative hours recover the hours that would have been reported for wage earners with missing eIncome data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper uses Statistics Denmark's own imputation method (hot-decking on group characteristics for wage earners; a salary-based hours calculation from tax returns for non-wage earners) and reports the level of detail attained

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed respondents with no administrative hours and a negative income on their tax return (5% of non-wage earners) are assumed not to have worked undeclared
The hours of the self-employed are overestimated in the survey by 9.8%, the negative adjustment Denmark applies to the reported hours of the self-employed in the National Accounts
key_assumptions.supported_by: OECD (2018:42): Denmark is one of five OECD countries that make negative adjustments to the reported hours of the self-employed

key_assumptions.assumption: Statistics Denmark's National Accounts gross value added per full-time employee by industry sector applies to the undeclared hours, and the same value added per hour applies to wage earners and non-wage earners
Undeclared hours are allocated to the industry sector of the respondent's main occupation
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper flags this as a limitation: only about 50% of those who report undeclared work in construction in Statistics Denmark's direct measure have construction as their main occupation, and for 6% of the employed population the secondary occupation is in a different sector

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours
Extreme survey values: under 1% of the sample works 75 or more hours a week and respondents, especially the self-employed, tend to overestimate hours
Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered
For the 10% of the employed population with flexible working hours and more actual than contracted hours, official additional hours cannot be disentangled from undeclared hours
Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week
Industry coding of undeclared work rests on the respondent's own description of the workplace and on the main occupation

estimator.value: descriptive tabulation of the labor input discrepancy (survey hours minus administrative hours); no regression model is estimated

estimation.specification: Labor input method: undeclared hours = corrected actual hours reported in the LFS reference week (scaled by 13 to a quarter) minus corrected eIncome administrative hours for the quarter, computed separately for main and secondary occupation and combined under the four-case rule set in the appendix section 'Methodology - calculating a discrepancy'. The paper prints no estimating equation for this quantity.
estimation.weights: Statistics Denmark LFS population weights scaling the quarterly data up to the general population

source_table.value: Table 5, row 'Total', 2015

nodes: application of the labor input method to individual-level LFS data linked to eIncome administrative tax data, with all four corrections applied
gross value added of the undeclared hours of wage earners, in million DKK at current prices

edges.from: employed and registered in the Danish population registers
edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

edges.from: absence for the whole LFS reference week
edges.to: inclusion in the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

edges.from: employer-side undeclared work
edges.to: public-sector gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome administrative hours

ambiguities: Table 5's 2015 column head reads 'gross value added of missing FTEs' while the 2014 column head reads 'missing hours'; the text treats both as the value of the undeclared hours.

evidence.exhibit: Table 5, row 'Total', column '2015 gross value added of missing FTEs in million DKK in current prices'

evidence.how: The paper reports no standard errors, confidence intervals or p-values for any estimate; Tables 1-9 and A1-A4 and Charts 1-3 print point values only.
The paper prints no standard deviation of the outcome anywhere; there is no summary-statistics table.

key_assumptions.supported_by: OECD (2018:42): Denmark is one of five OECD countries that make negative adjustments to the reported hours of the self-employed

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours
Extreme survey values: under 1% of the sample works 75 or more hours a week and respondents, especially the self-employed, tend to overestimate hours
Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered

Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week

claims.statement: Applying imputation of missing administrative hours for non-wage earners using tax-return income lowers the estimated proportion with undeclared work of non-wage earners in 2015 by 21 percentage points.

treatment.label: imputation of missing administrative hours for non-wage earners using tax-return income

register_source.value: Danish tax returns of the self-employed, added anonymously to the linked dataset by Statistics Denmark; no DST variable name is given

definition.value: For the two thirds of non-wage earners without eIncome data, salaried hours are calculated as (salary / average hourly wage for the group) * (calendar days in month / job length per month in calendar days), with 365 days substituted for calendar days because tax returns are annual, the group defined by age and gender, and the group hourly wage and average job length taken from the 44% of non-wage earners who meet Statistics Denmark's imputation-group criteria. timing.value: applied to the 2014 and 2015 data before the labor input discrepancy is calculated

outcome.label: percentage of non-wage earners with undeclared work

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: LFS-weighted share of non-wage earners for whom the labor input discrepancy calculation yields a positive number of undeclared hours, i.e. more corrected actual LFS hours than corrected eIncome administrative hours in the main and/or secondary occupation

timing.value: per calendar year, pooling the four quarters of the year

units.value: percentage points (change in the estimated proportion with undeclared work)

population.description: Non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers) among the employed respondents of the Danish Labor Force Survey 2014-2015 (approximately 6000 unique persons; 9% of the employed population), linked to eIncome data and to tax returns
subgroups_defined: wage earners
non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers)
industry sector of main occupation (NACE letter groups)
calendar quarter
population.selection: LFS respondents who are employed (persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour); cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (<1% of the employed population) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data; respondents absent for the whole reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

identification.source_of_variation: none - the estimate is a discrepancy between two measurements of the same person's hours (the LFS actual-hours answer and the eIncome hours reported by the employer), not exogenous variation

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper uses Statistics Denmark's own imputation method (hot-decking on group characteristics for wage earners; a salary-based hours calculation from tax returns for non-wage earners) and reports the level of detail attained

Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours

Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered

Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week
Industry coding of undeclared work rests on the respondent's own description of the workplace and on the main occupation

claims.statement: Applying correction of measurement error in the eIncome administrative hours of wage earners, benchmarked on the public sector lowers the estimated proportion with undeclared work of wage earners in 2015 by 26 percentage points.

treatment.label: correction of measurement error in the eIncome administrative hours of wage earners, benchmarked on the public sector

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: Within public-sector workers, the mean difference between the contracted hours reported in the LFS and the eIncome hours is computed for detailed groups (level 8: gender, scope of working hours, age group and workplace position; at least 50 people per group for 88% of public-sector workers) and this mean group difference is deducted from each person's eIncome hours before the undeclared hours are calculated.

timing.value: applied to the 2014 and 2015 data before the labor input discrepancy is calculated

outcome.label: percentage of wage earners with undeclared work

register_source.value: Danish Labor Force Survey (AKU) actual-hours question linked at the individual level to eIncome (eIndkomst) administrative hours; no DST variable names are given in the paper

definition.value: LFS-weighted share of wage earners for whom the labor input discrepancy calculation yields a positive number of undeclared hours, i.e. more corrected actual LFS hours than corrected eIncome administrative hours in the main and/or secondary occupation

timing.value: per calendar year, pooling the four quarters of the year

units.value: percentage points (change in the estimated proportion with undeclared work)

estimand.target_population: the paper's own 2015 estimate of undeclared work for wage earners; the quantity is the change in that estimate produced by the correction

population.description: Wage earners among the employed respondents of the Danish Labor Force Survey 2014-2015 (approximately 54,000 unique persons; 91% of the employed population), linked to eIncome administrative tax data
subgroups_defined: wage earners
non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers)
industry sector of main occupation (NACE letter groups)
calendar quarter
population.selection: LFS respondents who are employed (persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour); cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (<1% of the employed population) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data; respondents absent for the whole reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

identification.source_of_variation: none - the estimate is a discrepancy between two measurements of the same person's hours (the LFS actual-hours answer and the eIncome hours reported by the employer), not exogenous variation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents have no reason to conceal their undeclared working hours in a household / labor force survey, so the hours they report include all hours worked, undeclared hours included
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the survey must be run by an institution unassociated with the tax authority, and notes that Statistics Denmark administers the Danish LFS and is completely unassociated with the tax office; it also notes that interviewers persist when a respondent answers 0 hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The residual between survey hours and administrative hours is assumed to represent undeclared working hours

The estimate is conditioned on being employed and registered in the official Danish population registers; the method does not cover undeclared work by populations outside formal employment, including undocumented workers, nor cross-border workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper bounds the size of the excluded undocumented population (Larsen and Skaksen 2019 estimate around 18,000 persons in 2015 against an employed population of about 2.5 million) and removes the under-1% of respondents who live in Denmark but work abroad

implies_edges.from: employed and registered in the Danish population registers
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents with fewer actual survey hours than administrative hours are assumed not to have worked any undeclared hours
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes the method cannot detect undeclared work for this group and accepts the resulting underestimation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who state flexible / shifting working hours as the reason for additional hours are assumed to be working legitimately, so their additional hours are not counted as undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: Looking at the direct measure of undeclared work in the survey, this group of people are not more likely to have engaged in undeclared work

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who worked 0 actual LFS hours because they were on leave for the whole reference week are removed from the discrepancy calculation (only their secondary-occupation discrepancy is considered)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows in Table A3 that in 2015.3 there are more administrative hours than survey hours, and accepts that the estimate may be underestimated for this population

implies_edges.from: absence for the whole LFS reference week
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

key_assumptions.assumption: The gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome hours among public-sector workers does not capture undeclared work on the employer's side, so it can serve as a benchmark for measurement error in the administrative data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues there is no reason for public employers to underreport hours and salaries of wage earners to the tax authorities, and that it can be said with relative certainty that this discrepancy does not capture employer-side undeclared work

implies_edges.from: employer-side undeclared work
implies_edges.to: public-sector gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome administrative hours

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours
Extreme survey values: under 1% of the sample works 75 or more hours a week and respondents, especially the self-employed, tend to overestimate hours
Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered
For the 10% of the employed population with flexible working hours and more actual than contracted hours, official additional hours cannot be disentangled from undeclared hours
Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week
Industry coding of undeclared work rests on the respondent's own description of the workplace and on the main occupation

definition.value: LFS-weighted share of non-wage earners for whom the labor input discrepancy calculation yields a positive number of undeclared hours, i.e. more corrected actual LFS hours than corrected eIncome administrative hours in the main and/or secondary occupation

timing.value: per calendar year, pooling the four quarters of the year

units.value: percentage points (change in the estimated proportion with undeclared work)

estimand.target_population: the paper's own 2014 estimate of undeclared work for non-wage earners; the quantity is the change in that estimate produced by the correction

population.description: Non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers) among the employed respondents of the Danish Labor Force Survey 2014-2015 (approximately 6000 unique persons; 9% of the employed population), linked to eIncome data and to tax returns
subgroups_defined: wage earners
non-wage earners (self-employed, assisting spouses and contributing family workers)
industry sector of main occupation (NACE letter groups)
calendar quarter
population.selection: LFS respondents who are employed (persons who in a normal week would work at least one hour); cross-border workers who live in Denmark but work abroad (<1% of the employed population) are removed because they have no corresponding administrative data; respondents absent for the whole reference week are removed from the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

identification.source_of_variation: none - the estimate is a discrepancy between two measurements of the same person's hours (the LFS actual-hours answer and the eIncome hours reported by the employer), not exogenous variation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents have no reason to conceal their undeclared working hours in a household / labor force survey, so the hours they report include all hours worked, undeclared hours included
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the survey must be run by an institution unassociated with the tax authority, and notes that Statistics Denmark administers the Danish LFS and is completely unassociated with the tax office; it also notes that interviewers persist when a respondent answers 0 hours

key_assumptions.assumption: The residual between survey hours and administrative hours is assumed to represent undeclared working hours

The estimate is conditioned on being employed and registered in the official Danish population registers; the method does not cover undeclared work by populations outside formal employment, including undocumented workers, nor cross-border workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper bounds the size of the excluded undocumented population (Larsen and Skaksen 2019 estimate around 18,000 persons in 2015 against an employed population of about 2.5 million) and removes the under-1% of respondents who live in Denmark but work abroad

implies_edges.from: employed and registered in the Danish population registers
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents with fewer actual survey hours than administrative hours are assumed not to have worked any undeclared hours
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes the method cannot detect undeclared work for this group and accepts the resulting underestimation

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who state flexible / shifting working hours as the reason for additional hours are assumed to be working legitimately, so their additional hours are not counted as undeclared
key_assumptions.supported_by: Looking at the direct measure of undeclared work in the survey, this group of people are not more likely to have engaged in undeclared work

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents who worked 0 actual LFS hours because they were on leave for the whole reference week are removed from the discrepancy calculation (only their secondary-occupation discrepancy is considered)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows in Table A3 that in 2015.3 there are more administrative hours than survey hours, and accepts that the estimate may be underestimated for this population

implies_edges.from: absence for the whole LFS reference week
implies_edges.to: inclusion in the main-occupation discrepancy calculation

key_assumptions.assumption: The gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome hours among public-sector workers does not capture undeclared work on the employer's side, so it can serve as a benchmark for measurement error in the administrative data
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues there is no reason for public employers to underreport hours and salaries of wage earners to the tax authorities, and that it can be said with relative certainty that this discrepancy does not capture employer-side undeclared work

implies_edges.from: employer-side undeclared work
implies_edges.to: public-sector gap between contracted LFS hours and eIncome administrative hours

threats_discussed: Missing eIncome data (8-9% of respondents; 64% of the self-employed) would be counted as fully undeclared work in an aggregated approach
Legitimate overtime (7-8% of the employed population) would be counted as undeclared hours
Extreme survey values: under 1% of the sample works 75 or more hours a week and respondents, especially the self-employed, tend to overestimate hours
Errors in the administrative data: for 61% of wage earners the reported agreed hours differ from the eIncome hours by more than +/- 2 hours, including 36% of public-sector workers
Respondents round hours off, e.g. reporting 38 hours instead of 37.5 (Statistics Denmark, 2012)
Undeclared work is allocated to the industry of the respondent's main occupation, which need not be where it was performed
Administrative hours in secondary occupations have not been corrected, as there are too few observations for the imputation method
Full-week absences (about 12% of respondents in a normal quarter, 22% in the third quarter) cannot be detected in the administrative data
Lunchbreaks could disturb the discrepancy calculation; the paper examines paid and unpaid lunchbreaks and concludes no correction is needed
robustness_checks: Appendix Tables A1 and A2 report the estimate with all corrections, with no corrections, and leaving each correction out in turn
Validation against Statistics Denmark's direct undeclared-work question in the LFS (Section 5.4)
Comparison with Rockwool Foundation Research Unit questionnaire estimates and with Williams et al. (2017) and Pedersen (2003)
Stability of the industry-sector results across years and consecutive quarters (correlations of 0.98, 0.82 and 0.88)
An alternative extreme-value rule (top 5% set to the 95th percentile, Bentsen et al. 2018) is described and reported to give a lower estimate
unresolved_confounders: The method cannot separate employer-side undeclared work from errors in the eIncome administrative data; the public-sector benchmark correction removes both
Undeclared work by people outside formal employment, by undocumented workers and by cross-border workers is not covered
For the 10% of the employed population with flexible working hours and more actual than contracted hours, official additional hours cannot be disentangled from undeclared hours
Underestimation for respondents paid during national holidays and for respondents absent for the whole reference week
Industry coding of undeclared work rests on the respondent's own description of the workplace and on the main occupation

estimator.value: descriptive tabulation of the labor input discrepancy (survey hours minus administrative hours); no regression model is estimated

estimation.specification: Labor input method: undeclared hours = corrected actual hours reported in the LFS reference week (scaled by 13 to a quarter) minus corrected eIncome administrative hours for the quarter, computed separately for main and secondary occupation and combined under the four-case rule set in the appendix section 'Methodology - calculating a discrepancy'. The paper prints no estimating equation for this quantity.
estimation.weights: Statistics Denmark LFS population weights scaling the quarterly data up to the general population

source_table.value: Table A2 (appendix), row 'Average proportion with undeclared work in%. - 2014', columns 'With all corrections' and 'Without measurement error correction'

edges.to: inclusion in the estimation sample

ambiguities: baseline_mean is the level printed in Table A2 (appendix) under 'Without measurement error correction'; the point estimate is the change relative to it.
This is the effect of a methodological choice on the paper's own estimate, not an effect on any person; the graph edge records the tested analytical relationship.

evidence.how: The paper reports no standard errors, confidence intervals or p-values for any estimate; Tables 1-9 and A1-A4 and Charts 1-3 print point values only.
The paper prints no standard deviation of the outcome anywhere; there is no summary-statistics table.
Appendix Table A2, average proportion with undeclared work 2014: 37% with all corrections and 37% without the measurement error correction; the difference is 0 percentage points.
